newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Busang gold fears shock mining industry.
newsitem.headline: Busang gold fears shock mining industry.

text.p: Indonesia on Thursday put the Busang gold find on hold after the mining industry was rocked by news the lode might be nowhere near as rich as first reported.

The director-general of the mines and energy ministry, Kuntoro Mangkusubroto, told reporters he was putting aside applications for contracts of work by Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd to further explore and develop the property.
U.S. and Indonesian partners of the small Bre-X exploration company said their participation in developing Busang depended on how much gold the property actually contained.

Bre-X shocked the mining industry with a statement on Wednesday that the site in the rain forests of East Kalimantan province on Borneo island might hold far less than the 71 million ounces it had earlier declared.
"This could be an acute embarrassment to the government, especially with (May 29) general elections only a few weeks away," an industry source said.

Bre-X chief executive David Walsh said in a statement from Calgary: "There appears to be a strong possibility that the potential gold resources on the Busang property...have been overstated because of invalid samples and assaying of those samples."
Only last Monday Walsh had said he had "absolute confidence in the integrity and accuracy of assay results and resource calculations reported by the company".

Bre-X shares, suspended on Wednesday on the Toronto Stock Exchange, were hit last week by news that the company's chief geologist, Filipino Michael de Guzman, had fallen to his death from a helicopter over Kalimantan in an incident which some officials said could have been suicide.
That was followed last Friday by an Indonesian newspaper report casting doubt on the size of the Busang motherlode.

The Busang saga developed last year with ever-mounting reports on the amount of gold and a scramble by major mining companies for a slice of the property, billed as the biggest single find since gold was discovered on South Africa's Witwatersrand late last century.
The discovery, worth around $25 billion at current market prices, appeared to be a dream-come-true for Walsh, a 51-year-old Canadian ex-stockbroker who in 1993 sank Bre-X's last $10,000 into Busang.

Bre-X announced on February 17 the 71-million-ounce estimate and said it had teamed up with an Indonesian partner closely tied to President Suharto, and the U.S. Freeport-McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc to develop Busang after fighting off a bid by Canada's Barrick Gold Corp.
Members of Suharto's family were also closely involved in the in-fighting leading up to the final agreement and a senior Indonesian mining official was temporarily pushed aside.
Industry sources said the main potential losers were the Bre-X shareholders.

Freeport and the Indonesian partners are conducting a "due diligence" process -- a complete and careful scrutiny of Busang -- before commiting themselves further. No money has yet changed hands between the partners.
Freeport also said on Wednesday its own drilling results on Busang so far "indicate insignificant amounts of gold".
"I don't see any good coming out of this for anybody," one senior mining source said.
He said surveys of Busang were still continuing. Other mining sources said it was still unclear what had happened.
One source feared it might inhibit the government from granting contracts of work to small foreign companies who do the bulk of the exploration work in remote areas.

"That's normally where the big mining companies get their best leads from," he said. "We normally encourage the smaller guys to go in and then bring their finds to the attention of the big companies for development."
